source: Friedman, Chen & Vaid (2006) Proverb preferences across cultures: dialecticality or poeticality? Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 13(2):353-359
finding: Failed replication of the proverb part of Peng and Nisbett 1999. Used the same stimuli as their Experiment 2 plus a new set screened for equal phrasing. Chinese and American raters did not differ in preference for dialectical proverbs.
numbers: Chinese rated proverbs more familiar and (Set 1) more poetic than Americans; no group difference by dialecticality. Set 1: both groups rated the PN dialectical proverbs more liked, wiser, more poetic than nondialectical ones. Set 2: dialectical proverbs only as liked, wise and poetic as nondialectical. Sample sizes not in the abstract I read.
quote: Caution should be taken in ascribing differences in proverb preferences solely to cultural differences in reasoning.
limits: Only the PubMed abstract was read (full text not opened), so N per group is unknown. Tests only the proverb task, not the contradiction-plausibility or conflict-resolution tasks. Authors say poeticality confounded the original effect.
agent_relevance: The best-known proverb result is weak evidence. Treat the 1999 effect as a design spec for items, not as a measured human baseline. Control phrasing quality in any two-rules test set.

source: Spencer-Rodgers, Major-Siciliano, Yan, Cortijo, McKenzie & Peng (2026) The Dialectical Self Around the World: A Meta-Analysis of Country-Level Means. PSPB
finding: First meta-analysis of the Dialectical Self Scale. Country-level dialecticism clusters by region and tracks tolerance of contradiction and expectation of change. It is unrelated to collectivism and interdependent self-construal, so it is a separate mindset.
numbers: k=139 studies, N=23,629, 28 countries. No historical shift over two decades. Linked to Buddhism and rice farming; only weakly to globalization.
limits: Abstract only. Country-level means of a self-report scale, not reasoning performance. Not a replication of the 1999 reasoning tasks. No per-culture N or effect sizes read.
agent_relevance: Supports treating dialecticism as its own construct, not a proxy for collectivism. Says nothing on whether holding two rules improves reasoning.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Chi, Stafford, Collier & Vlachos (2026) Demystifying Multi-Agent Debate: The Role of Confidence and Diversity
finding: Vanilla debate (5 agents x 5 rounds) often loses to plain majority vote on small models. Seeding the debate with a more diverse pool of initial answers and sharing calibrated confidence beats majority vote.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B: GSM8K debate 0.847 vs majority vote 0.908 vs single 0.908; CommonsenseQA 0.727 vs 0.808; GPQA 0.339 vs 0.335. Llama-3.1-8B: GSM8K debate 0.850 vs vote 0.870; CSQA 0.688 vs 0.718. HD+Confidence: Qwen GSM8K 0.932, Llama MMLU-PM 0.842. Initial diversity vs debate gain: r=0.070 (Qwen) and 0.019 (Llama), n=26,624.
limits: Only 7-8B open models. Debate (25 calls) costs more than the vote it is compared with; gains of the new methods over vote are small (about 1-3 points).
agent_relevance: Keeping several different candidates alive helps only if they differ at the start and the choice uses calibrated confidence. Plain back-and-forth between copies of one model adds nothing over voting.

source: Zhang, Cui, Chen, Wang, Zhang, Wang, Wu & Hu (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five debate methods on 9 benchmarks and 4 models were compared with chain-of-thought and self-consistency at about 6 LLM calls. Debate mostly did not win, and self-consistency used extra tokens better.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: MMLU CoT 80.73, SC 82.13, SoM debate 74.73, EoT 67.87, ChatEval 79.13, AgentVerse 80.40; GSM8K CoT 93.60, SC 95.67, SoM 94.93. Across 36 configs (4 models x 9 sets) most debate methods beat CoT in only about 15% of cases (ANOVA, alpha .05). Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: only AgentVerse beat CoT (+0.85); others lower by 3.60 or more.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: Equal LLM calls, not equal tokens; the authors plot tokens separately (SC scales with more samples, debate does not). Mostly one-answer benchmarks. Models: GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8B/70B, Claude-3.5-haiku.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 9 for single-answer tasks: debate does not beat self-consistency at matched budget. Still silent on tasks where both rules are partly true.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing MAD - model heterogeneity result (Table 4)
finding: Mixing two different models inside a debate helped every debate method tried, which hints that the useful part of 'two views' is real diversity of source.
numbers: Heter-SoM vs the average of SoM run on each model alone: +6.4% mean over 9 benchmarks (HumanEval +15.3%, AGIEval +10.8%); vs CoT-average +5.8%. Heter-EoT +8.2% vs EoT-average, +4.4% vs CoT-average. Some sets negative vs CoT-average (MBPP -2.0 to -10.8, ARC-C -1.4).
limits: Only two model pairs; relative percent gains; cost of running two models not matched.
agent_relevance: A second rule or view should come from a different source (other model, retrieved text, tool), not from the same model told to disagree with itself.

source: Choi, Zhu & Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Across 7 benchmarks majority voting alone gives most of the gain credited to debate. A theory model shows debate preserves expected correctness (a martingale), so debate alone cannot raise it. Nudging updates toward correction helps.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B average accuracy: single agent 0.7205, majority vote 0.7691, best debate 0.7377 (Decentralized T=2); centralized debate 0.6551 to 0.6672. Arithmetic: vote 0.99 vs single 0.814. Llama3.1-8B average: single 0.6203, best debate 0.6990 (Sparse T=2). With Qwen2.5-32B the authors report vote still carries most of the gain.
limits: Small open models; 5 agents. Vote needs fewer calls than debate. Llama vote row was not extracted from the table.
agent_relevance: Holding both views open has no free lunch: unless the second view carries new information, the expected result equals sampling. Supports demanding an outside counterexample for S7.

source: Wu, Li & Li (2025) Can LLM Agents Really Debate? A Controlled Study of Multi-Agent Debate in Logical Reasoning
finding: Controlled debate study with verifiable truth. The main drivers of success are the intrinsic reasoning strength of agents and group diversity; order and confidence visibility matter little. Majority pressure suppresses independent correction, but good teams can overturn a wrong consensus.
numbers: No single headline number used. Six factors varied: team size, composition, confidence visibility, order, depth, task difficulty.
limits: Logic puzzles with one answer. Only the abstract, introduction and process claims were read, not all tables.
agent_relevance: A held-open minority rule survives only when the agent can judge validity; majority pressure is the failure mode S7 must guard against.

source: Hong, Byun, Kim, Shu & Choi (2025, v4 2026) Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues (SYCON-Bench)
finding: 17 LLMs, three scenarios, up to 5 turns of user pressure. Bigger and reasoning models hold their stance longer. A third-person framing prompt cuts flipping.
numbers: Debate scenario, turns held before flipping (ToF, max about 5) and number of flips (NoF): o3-mini 4.97 / 0.01; DeepSeek-r1 4.85 / 0.08; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct 4.90 / 0.02; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 0.83 / 2.63; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 2.44 / 1.94. Third-person prompt: up to 63.8% more ToF in debate; plus an anti-sycophancy line: up to 28% in unethical queries. Larger models cut sycophancy by up to 81.4%, reasoning models by up to 21.6%.
limits: Measures stance holding on opinion and debate prompts, not whether the held stance is correct. GPT-4o judge checked against humans on 100 items per scenario for one model. Table text was garbled in extraction, so only the figures quoted are used.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 in part: strong models rarely flip within 5 turns of casual pressure, small models flip often. A third-person 'what would a neutral reviewer say' wording is a cheap guardrail for S7.

source: Shah (2026) The Silicon Mirror: Dynamic Behavioral Gating for Anti-Sycophancy in LLM Agents
finding: A gating plus critic-rewrite layer cut sycophancy on adversarial TruthfulQA prompts.
numbers: 437 TruthfulQA adversarial scenarios. Claude Sonnet 4 baseline sycophancy 9.6% to 1.4% (85.7% relative cut, p<1e-6, OR 7.64). Gemini 2.5 Flash 46.0% to 14.2% (OR 5.15).
limits: Single independent author; abstract and introduction read; scenarios scripted; LLM-graded; not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A critic step that audits for caving can cut flips by large factors, but baseline sycophancy varies about 5x between models.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou & Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Models commit to an answer too early when information arrives in pieces, then rely on that answer. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) are no better.
numbers: Average drop 39% over six tasks, single-turn vs multi-turn. Aptitude -15 to -16%, unreliability +112%. First answer attempt in the first 20% of the conversation: mean score 30.9; in the last 20%: 64.4 (Code and Math). Final answers 20-300% longer in sharded runs. Reasoning models' replies about 33% longer. 200,000+ simulated conversations.
limits: Underspecified instructions revealed over turns, not a fixed two-rule problem. Means pooled across models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 8: committing to one rule early costs about half the score when evidence is still arriving. S7 should defer commitment until a deciding observation arrives and allow a restart from a recap.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing (ICLR)
finding: A real checker (code interpreter, search) recovers about half of the gain an oracle would give. Self-critique without the tool helps a little on ChatGPT but hurt text-davinci-003.
numbers: GSM8k ChatGPT, Table 10: PoT 72.5; +CRITIC 78.2 (+5.7); oracle (correct only wrong answers) 83.9 (+11.4); CRITIC without tool 77.0 (+4.5). Text-davinci-003: +1.1 with tool, oracle +7.3, no tool -1.8. LLaMA-2-70B: GSM8k +3.0 vs oracle +12.7; TabMWP PoT 59.0, CRITIC 75.0 (+16), oracle 92.0 (+32.3).
limits: Main-text Table 2 rows were scrambled in extraction; Table 10 (clean) used for ChatGPT. Program-of-thought setting where errors show as execution output.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: a realistic tool checker gets about 30-50% of the oracle gain (5.7 of 11.4 on GSM8k ChatGPT; 16 of 32.3 on TabMWP 70B). Oracle numbers are an upper bound, not a target.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han & Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from the same prompted LLM, except on tasks exceptionally suited for it. Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Qualitative survey; many reported gains rely on oracle information or weak initial prompts (see their checklist).
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey, not a new experiment; abstract and introduction read in detail.
agent_relevance: S7 needs a named external signal for the counterexample; self-critique alone is not it.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli & Zhou (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (ICLR)
finding: Execution results and unit tests as feedback let the model repair its code. Explaining the code in words helps even when no tests exist.
numbers: Spider (no unit tests): +2 to +3%, and +9% on the hardest level, with code explanation. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Matches or beats baselines that sample more than 10x candidates.
limits: Code tasks where a test can be run; 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: A test case is the cleanest counterexample. Feedback reuse is more sample-efficient than drawing many candidates, which is the equal-token comparison S7 needs.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, Sclar, Pyatkin, Bhagavatula, Wang, Kim, Choi, Dziri & Ren (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning of LMs with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR)
finding: Closest existing test of S7's design: GPT-4 proposes several candidate rules, a symbolic interpreter checks them against examples, and failing rules are refined. It beats direct prompting, self-consistency and self-refine on 3 of 4 datasets, but the model cannot reliably apply the rules it proposes.
numbers: GPT-4. ACRE raw accuracy: IO 64.0, SC (N=5) 65.0, Self-Refine 70.0, refinement T=3,N=5 82.5; ACRE task accuracy IO 28.0, SC 29.0, SR 32.0, refinement T=1,N=5 48.0, T=3,N=5 59.0. MiniARC raw accuracy lags IO (refinement 18.7 vs IO 33.1). Rule-application gap: task accuracy falls from more than 80% to near zero on MiniSCAN when the LM applies its own rule.
limits: A symbolic interpreter supplies the counterexamples; the pure-LM Self-Refine baseline gains little. Table rows for MiniSCAN and List Functions were scrambled, so only ACRE and MiniARC cells are quoted. Not framed as dialectics.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gaps 1 and 2: keeping N candidate rules and killing them only on a failed example works when a checker exists. It does not test the 'both rules partly true' case.

source: Li, Wu, Ji, Zhang, Fei, Zhang, Lee & Hsu (2026) Taming Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Agents via Dialectical Alignment (ReTAS)
finding: Agents swap their blame for a failure when the role changes (self-reflection vs audit). A Qwen3-4B model trained with thesis-antithesis-synthesis chain of thought and RL beats larger open models on consistency. Merely adding an opposing reviewer role did not help and sometimes hurt.
numbers: Role swap triggers the bias in over 20% of cases for most models; GPT-5.1 about 5%. FinQA-TAS: ReTAS 4B Acc 71.2, Flip 12.4 vs QwQ-32B dual view 54.9 / 18.1, Qwen3-30B-A3B 52.9 / 20.1, GLM-4.6 43.1 / 52.7. Spider-TAS Acc 61.4. Dual View was worse than Single View for GLM-4.6.
limits: This is training, not a prompt scaffold; our agent cannot train. Benchmark built by the authors with an LLM generator. Closed models still win on absolute F1.
agent_relevance: Adding a critic with the opposite role is not enough; the synthesis step and a consistency check across perspectives matter. Supports a perspective-swap test inside S7.

source: Candussio (2026) A Dialectic Pipeline for Improving LLM Robustness (MSc thesis) - model list
finding: Checked which models the antithesis gains were measured on. The thesis uses small open models (Phi-3 mini and medium, Gemma-2 2B and 9B, Llama 8B), with Phi-3-mini producing the alternative answers.
numbers: No frontier model and no equal-token comparison found in the setup; gain sizes are already logged as c16 and c17 (WikiHop +11.6, +10.6, +15.6 over CoT).
limits: Thesis, one author; model list and setup read, but the absence claim comes from reading setup sections, not an exhaustive text search.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays negative: the antithesis gain has not been shown at equal tokens for strong models. Pair with Abbasloo (b21), where GPT-5 synthesis moved little.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - oracle versus no-oracle, tied to CRITIC
finding: Oracle labels inflate self-correction results. Without them, self-correction lowers accuracy on CommonSenseQA.
numbers: GSM8K with oracle: GPT-3.5 75.9 to 95.5, GPT-4 84.3 to 97.5. Without oracle: GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 89.7 to 85.5. Compare d11: a real code interpreter gave +5.7 of the +11.4 oracle gain for ChatGPT.
limits: Re-read of c20 and c25 to tie the numbers together; no new experiment.
agent_relevance: The oracle gain (13 to 20 points) is an upper bound. A checker that can run code or tests recovers roughly a third to a half; a checker that is the same model recovers nothing.

source: Chan (2000) Formal logic and dialectical thinking are not incongruent; Ho (2000) Dialectical thinking: neither eastern nor western. American Psychologist 55(9):1063-1065
finding: Two published comments on Peng and Nisbett 1999 argue that dialectical thinking and formal logic are compatible, and that dialectical thinking is not specifically Eastern or Western.
numbers: No data. PubMed records only (titles, authors, journal).
limits: Only the PubMed records were read, not the comment text; the argument is inferred from titles.
agent_relevance: Fits the weak-subfacet finding: 'dialectical' covers several things. S7 need not set logic against dialectics; a counterexample test is itself formal.

source: Search log for gaps 5 and 7 (null result)
finding: A PubMed search for replications of Peng and Nisbett 1999 plus two web searches (replication with large N; LLM Dialectical Self Scale rerun) found only Friedman et al. 2006 (failed proverb replication). No replication with N>=300 per culture of the contradiction-plausibility task, and no rerun of Jin et al. 2023 with 30-60 items, was found.
numbers: Searches on 2026-11-03: one PubMed esearch (1 hit, an unrelated paper), two WebSearch calls. The arXiv API returned empty results for the later queries.
limits: Absence of evidence in a few searches, not proof. The arXiv outage limited the LLM-side search.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 7 stay open; plan a small own test rather than rely on the literature.
